members.tone: The plain word, and one of the few virtues nobody argues about.
Carries a trace of prayer - thanks owed to providence as much as to a person.
Cooler and more measured; it values the thing rather than feeling the debt.
The weakest claim here, and the one most easily said out of politeness.
States the position without explaining it - the trust is simply absent.
Assumes the worst motive as a general rule, which saves the trouble of looking.
The furthest word here: not distrust of a person but of the species.
The longer form of the same judgement, and rarer.
Describes a state of mind, and doubt is not a fault in itself.
Nearly neutral - in most contexts it is what a careful person does.
A vice socially and a virtue scientifically; the field decides the charge.
The British spelling, identical in force.
Fear of being displaced. The older sense - jealous of one's honour - was closer to vigilance.
Shakespeare's monster, and the phrase has outlived the play.
Marks the excess explicitly, which suggests some jealousy was warranted.
Informal and wary rather than hostile; it expects a trick, not a betrayal.
The plainer twin of *distrustful*, and a shade more tentative.
Cuts both ways - a suspicious person and a suspicious package are opposite roles.
Built as a plain negative, and it sounds like a diagnosis.
Usually prudence rather than fault; wariness is what experience leaves behind.
Warm and forward-looking; the desire is presented as a credit to the person.
This sense means *eagerly desirous* - *anxious to help* - and is easily misread as worry.
*Dying to know* - hyperbole so complete that no one hears the death in it.
Enthusiasm at temperature; usually about a thing rather than a task.
The same energy with the waiting resented - eagerness that has turned on its object.
Only in *raring to go*, and it is nearly always approving.
Names the excess, and implies the eagerness spoiled what it wanted.
Approving of the mind and faintly wary of the manner - the gloss admits both.
Praise for a child, and a hint of too many questions for an adult.
Curiosity aimed at ideas rather than people, and neutral for it.
The plainest form: the questions are being asked, and nothing is implied about why.
Curiosity with the wonder still in it, and no agenda attached.
The everyday accusation, and it is about other people's business specifically.
The alternative spelling, equally common.
Names the act rather than the character - the person is doing it right now.
Informal and slightly comic, which takes some of the sting out.
The formal way of saying nosy, and it grants that curiosity itself was fine.
A dictionary word rather than a spoken one; it names the absence and stops.
Neutral in the balance - a strict teacher is a complaint or a compliment depending on the year.
Bare rather than harsh, and in architecture and prose it is often praise.
The face more than the rule; sternness is something the other person can see.
As in *blue laws* - Sabbath strictness, now almost entirely historical.
Borrows a whole religious movement to say *no pleasure allowed*.
The commoner form, and now used almost exclusively as an accusation.
Institutional and euphemistic - it is what discipline is called in a report.
Used of measures for correcting or punishing misconduct.
The rarer variant, and no less procedural.
Self-denial by vocation, and slightly mocking when applied outside a monastery.
Technical, and at home in writing about religion rather than character.
The adjectival twin, equally confined to the same writing.
Formal to the point of coldness - it describes the giving up, not the reason.
The same restraint, warmed by the suggestion that it was chosen.
The virtue the family arrives at: restraint that answers to nobody else.
Places the fault in the nature, which leaves no room for a bad day.
Black bile, straight from the four humours; unusable now without irony.
The same medicine, still current, and it makes the temper sound like a symptom.
Now aimed mostly at critics and prose styles, where it is half a compliment.
British and dated - the liver as the seat of a bad mood.
The animal image is doing the work: approach and something goes up.
Touchy about a particular subject rather than in general.
Another organ, another temper, and the most literary of the set.
Small, quick and stinging - it describes the remarks more than the mood.
Almost affectionate when said of the old, which no other word here manages.
Difficulty over small things, and comic rather than frightening.
American and fond as often as not; an ornery mule is being described, not blamed.
The fourth humour. Anger arrives fast and is presented as constitutional.
The formal word for a short fuse, and the most neutral in tone.
Anger plus poor judgement - the heat is in the thinking.
The plain compound, and the one most likely to be said out loud.
Comparative and cold - it needs something better to exist before it means anything.
The broadest word in English doing narrow work: below average, and nothing more.
Of metals, where it is technical. The moral sense is a separate and much older word.
American and dismissive - *a bum deal*, *a bum knee*.
Price used as a verdict on quality, which is the oldest trick in the word.
Often affectionate about films and pop songs; the badness is part of the appeal.
Named for chintz fabric, and it still smells faintly of the furnishings.
Plain and unliterary, and it complains about the thing rather than sneering at it.
Dated slang for poor quality, long since overtaken by the music.
Adds moral squalor to shoddiness - the thing is cheap and slightly corrupt.
Specific to sound, and precise enough to be almost neutral.
From minor-league baseball, and the condescension is built in.
The clipped form, and rarer outside American speech.
A cheapjack was a travelling seller of trash; the person came first.
Shoddy was reclaimed wool sold as new, so the word began as a fraud.
From St Audrey's lace, sold cheap at her fair - gaudiness and cheapness together.
The plain complaint, and a mild one - noise is expected in most places.
Has largely left sound behind; *blatant* now means flagrant, and the loudness is figurative.
Literary and rare, and usually about demands rather than volume.
A crowd word - many voices at once, insisting on something.
Aimed at women's voices far more often than men's, which is worth knowing before using it.
Frequently approving: vociferous support is a compliment to the supporter.
Pleasant far more often than not - a room abuzz is a room going well.
The same sound, and equally likely to describe excitement as annoyance.
Metallic and resonant; the word is mostly used to make prose sound loud.
The plain form, and it names the sound without judging it much.
Harder and duller than clanging - chains and machinery rather than bells.
Small hard things in quantity; kitchens and typewriters.
Also used of arguments and institutions, where it means old and barely holding.
The rarer and shriller variant, and it sounds like what it means.
Old-fashioned and slightly fond, as of children.
Noise as a good time - *a rip-roaring success* has no complaint in it at all.
Neutral and factual; use leaves marks, and the word says only that.
The geological sense - a landscape at an advanced stage of erosion.
Technical and rare, from the same root as *attrition*.
Implies force rather than time, and of a person it means something much worse.
British, and it works equally on a car, a machine or a person - which is the joke.
The sound stands in for the condition; it suggests one more use might be too many.
Broken down past repair, and cruel when turned on a person.
Abandoned as well as ruined - nobody is coming back for it.
Contemptuous and vivid; it adds squalor to mere wear.
Of buildings and neighbourhoods mostly, where it carries an accusation about neglect.
Describes the look of sorrow rather than the damage, which makes it oddly gentle.
The one word here that is nearly affectionate - a dog-eared book was loved.
The clipped form, and rare enough to be mistaken for the anatomy word.
Geological and neutral; erosion is a process, not a fault.
Worn by water or wind, and the same word means thoroughly cleaned.
Edges only, and forgiving - *frayed nerves* borrows exactly that mildness.
